definition:
The doctrine of judgment is the Bible's teaching that God, because he is good, does not ignore evil. He sees every deed, weighs it truly, and acts: in history, against nations and individuals, and at the end, when he will judge the whole world in righteousness through Jesus Christ. For a modern reader ‘judgment’ usually means condemnation. In Scripture it is wider. To judge is to set things right, which means both condemning the oppressor and rescuing the oppressed. That is why the Psalms can call the trees of the forest to sing because the LORD “is coming to judge the earth” (Psalm 96:13), and why the widow, the orphan, the poor, and the stranger appear again and again as the people whose cause God takes up. His justice begins with his own people: the prophets held Israel to God's standard before they turned to the nations, and the New Testament says judgment begins “with the family of God” (1 Peter 4:17).

The Hebrew vocabulary shows this breadth. The verb shaphat means ‘to judge’, but also ‘to govern’ and ‘to deliver’; the ‘judges’ of the book of Judges were mostly rescuers and rulers, not courtroom officials (Judges 2:16). Its noun mishpat can mean a verdict, a legal case, a custom, or the right order of things, including the rights owed to the weak. It is often paired with tsedaqah, ‘righteousness’, the quality of being in right relation and acting faithfully within it. The verb din means ‘to plead a cause’ or ‘to vindicate’; Jeremiah says King Josiah pleaded the cause (din) of the poor and needy, and asks, “Is this not what it means to know Me?” (Jeremiah 22:16). In the New Testament, krinō means ‘to judge’ or ‘decide’ and can lean toward ‘condemn’; krisis is the act of judging (and sometimes ‘justice’, as in Matthew 23:23), and krima is the verdict. Paul coins dikaiokrisia, ‘righteous judgment’, for the day of wrath (Romans 2:5). The bēma was the raised platform from which a magistrate gave judgment, like the one before which Paul stood in Corinth (Acts 18:12), and Paul uses it for “the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). What happens to those finally condemned has its own study (Hell and Final Destinies), and God's particular care for the poor has another (Justice, the Poor, and the Stranger).
ot:
Judgment enters the Bible's story as soon as sin does, and it comes mixed with mercy from the start. God warned that eating from the forbidden tree would bring death (Genesis 2:17), and after the first sin he pronounces sentences on the serpent, the woman, and the man (Genesis 3:14-19), yet he also clothes them (Genesis 3:21) and promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15). When Cain kills Abel, God says, “The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). That sentence sets a pattern: judgment in Scripture is often God's answer to the cry of a victim. The flood (Genesis 6 and 7) and the fire on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24) become the Bible's standing examples of judgment on a whole society, and between them stands Abraham's question as he pleads for Sodom: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25). The whole Bible assumes the answer is yes, and much of it wrestles with what that means when the world looks otherwise.

The exodus is judgment and salvation at once. God says that on Passover night “I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt” (Exodus 12:12), and in the same act he frees a people of slaves. The law that follows builds God's justice into Israel's common life. Judges must not take bribes or show partiality (Deuteronomy 16:18-20), because God himself is the one who shows “no partiality” and “executes justice for the fatherless and widow” (Deuteronomy 10:17-18). If Israel mistreats the widow and the orphan, “they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry” (Exodus 22:23). When God proclaims his name to Moses he is “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger”, yet “He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished” (Exodus 34:6-7). Israel's king was to embody this justice; Psalm 72 prays that he will “vindicate the afflicted among the people” and “crush the oppressor” (Psalm 72:4). The Psalms make judgment a matter of worship and of lament. God “judges the world with justice” (Psalm 9:8), and in Psalm 82 he stands in the divine assembly to condemn rulers who “judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked” and fail to “defend the cause of the weak and fatherless” (Psalm 82:2-3). But the psalmists also cry “how long will the wicked exult?” (Psalm 94:3), and Psalm 73 confesses near-despair at the prosperity of the wicked until the writer entered God's sanctuary: “then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17).

The prophets turn the doctrine on God's own people first. Amos opens with oracles against the surrounding nations and then turns on Judah and Israel, and he gives the reason: “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). Privilege increases accountability. What God wants is summed up in three lines: “let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24), to “seek justice and correct the oppressor” (Isaiah 1:17), and “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). Isaiah's song of the vineyard ends with a wordplay in Hebrew: God looked for mishpat, justice, and found mispach, bloodshed; for tsedaqah, righteousness, and heard tseʿaqah, a cry (Isaiah 5:7). The fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722 BC and of Jerusalem to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC were read by the prophets and the historians of Kings as God's judgment for idolatry and injustice (2 Kings 17:18), though never as his last word. Habakkuk protests that God seems to tolerate violence (Habakkuk 1:2-4) and is told to wait, for the vision “will surely come” (Habakkuk 2:3). Ezekiel insists that each person answers for his own ways and that God takes “no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11).

The hope sharpens toward a final judgment. The coming king from Jesse's line will not judge by appearances, “but with righteousness He will judge the poor” (Isaiah 11:4), and the Servant of the LORD “will bring justice to the nations” (Isaiah 42:1) without breaking a bruised reed. The Day of the LORD will come against all the proud. In Daniel's vision of the heavenly court “the books were opened” (Daniel 7:10), and the beastly empires lose their power while dominion is given to one like a son of man. Daniel 12:2 joins judgment to resurrection: the dead will awake, “some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.” Ecclesiastes ends its search for meaning with the same conviction: “God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14).
nt:
John the Baptist announces that “the axe lies ready at the root of the trees” (Matthew 3:10) and that the one coming after him holds a winnowing fork. Jesus' own teaching both deepens the judgment and relocates it. He says people will give account “for every careless word they have spoken” (Matthew 12:36). He teaches that judgment is proportioned to knowledge and privilege: it will be “more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment” than for the towns that saw his miracles and did not repent (Matthew 11:22), and the servant who knew his master's will is beaten with many blows, the one who did not with few (Luke 12:47-48). In the parable of the wheat and the weeds, judgment is deferred to the harvest (Matthew 13:30), which is why his followers are not to uproot others now. He forbids the condemning judgment of others that sets oneself above them (Matthew 7:1-2) while demanding discernment. Most striking, he claims the role of judge for himself. The Father “has assigned all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), and at the end all who are in the graves will hear his voice and come out “to the resurrection of life” or “to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:29). In the scene of the sheep and the goats, the Son of Man on his throne judges the nations by what they did for “the least of these brothers of Mine” (Matthew 25:40), identifying himself with the hungry, the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner.

John's Gospel adds that judgment has already begun. God did not send the Son to condemn the world but to save it, and yet “this is the verdict: The Light has come into the world, but men loved the darkness rather than the Light” (John 3:19). The one who believes “will not come under judgment” and “has crossed over from death to life” (John 5:24). The last day will publish a verdict already being given in each person's response to Jesus. The apostles preached this. Peter tells Cornelius that Jesus is “the One appointed by God to judge the living and the dead” (Acts 10:42), and Paul tells the philosophers in Athens that God “has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed”, and has given proof by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The resurrection is the public guarantee that the judgment is coming and names the judge.

Paul's letter to the Romans gives the fullest account. The wrath of God “is being revealed” now against godlessness (Romans 1:18), as God hands people over to what they have chosen. Then Paul turns on the reader who condemns others while doing the same things (Romans 2:1). On the day of wrath God “will repay each one according to his deeds” (Romans 2:6), without favoritism, judging Jew and Gentile alike by the light each had, including the law written on the heart and conscience, and he will “judge men's secrets through Christ Jesus” (Romans 2:16). The result is that “every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God” (Romans 3:19). The answer is not a lowering of the standard but the cross, where God put forward Christ as an atoning sacrifice “so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). So “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Yet believers still appear before Christ's judgment seat, “that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10; Romans 14:10-12). For them the judgment tests the quality of their work: what survives brings reward, what burns brings loss, while the person “will be saved, but only as if through the flames” (1 Corinthians 3:15). The Lord “will expose the motives of men's hearts” and then each will receive praise from God (1 Corinthians 4:5). Because God will judge, Christians must not take revenge but “leave room for God's wrath” (Romans 12:19).

The rest of the New Testament keeps both notes. Hebrews warns that for those who deliberately reject Christ there remains “a fearful expectation of judgment” (Hebrews 10:27), and that man is appointed to die once “and after that to face judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). James says that “judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment” (James 2:13). In Revelation the martyrs under the altar cry, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?” (Revelation 6:10), and heaven rejoices when Babylon, the city that grew rich on violence, falls, because “His judgments are true and just” (Revelation 19:2). At the end a great white throne appears, the books are opened with the book of life, and “the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books” (Revelation 20:12). The whole biblical story ends in a court, and in the same book the judge is the Lamb who was slain.

keyTexts.why: Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth will do what is right. The whole Bible assumes he will, and much of it wrestles with how.
God's own description of his name holds mercy and justice together: slow to anger and forgiving, yet by no means leaving the guilty unpunished.
God shows no partiality, takes no bribe, and executes justice for the fatherless and the widow. Israel's courts were to copy the divine judge.
God judges the rulers who fail the weak and the fatherless, and the psalm ends with a prayer for God to rise and judge the earth.
Creation rejoices because the LORD is coming to judge the world in righteousness. Judgment is good news for a wronged world.
The coming king from Jesse's line judges the poor with righteousness and not by appearances. The Messiah is promised as the just judge.
The Day of the LORD will be darkness for a people who worship while practicing injustice. God wants justice to roll like a river.
The heavenly court sits and the books are opened; the beastly empires lose their power and dominion is given to one like a son of man.
The Son of Man judges the nations by how they treated the least of his brothers, and the outcomes are eternal life and eternal punishment.
The Father has given all judgment to the Son. Whoever believes has already passed from death to life, and at the last day all the dead will rise to life or to judgment.
God has fixed a day to judge the world by the man he appointed and has given proof by raising him from the dead. The resurrection guarantees the judgment.
God judges impartially, according to deeds and to the light each person had, through Christ, and he judges the secrets of the heart.
The work of believers will be tested by fire; some will receive reward and some will suffer loss while still being saved.
All must appear before the judgment seat of Christ to receive what is due for what was done in the body. Believers are not exempt from giving account.
At the great white throne the dead are judged according to their deeds, and the book of life decides the outcome.

history:
The early church confessed the judgment in its first creeds: the Old Roman creed and the Apostles' Creed that grew from it say Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, as do the Creed of Nicaea (325) and its revision at Constantinople (381). The Athanasian Creed, a Latin statement probably from the late fifth or sixth century, adds that at his coming all people will rise with their bodies and give account for their own deeds. The first great challenge came from Marcion, a second-century teacher expelled by the church at Rome around 144, who separated the just and wrathful God of the Old Testament from the merciful Father of Jesus. The church answered by keeping both testaments and confessing one God who is both just and merciful, which is the reason the doctrine of judgment has never been treated as an embarrassment to be left behind in the Old Testament. Augustine, in books 20 and 21 of The City of God (413 to 426), argued that God's judgments in this life are often hidden, so that good and evil befall good and bad alike, and that the last judgment will show the justice of all his judgments.

The medieval church made the judgment one of the four last things (death, judgment, heaven, and hell) and painted it over church doors and chancel arches. The thirteenth-century Dies Irae, sung at requiem masses for centuries, and Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel (1536 to 1541) gave it lasting form. The same period developed the teaching that good works done in grace merit reward, which the Council of Trent restated in its decree on justification (1547). The Reformation turned on how a sinner can stand before the judge. Martin Luther, in the preface to his Latin writings (1545), recalled that he had hated the phrase ‘the righteousness of God’ because he took it to mean the justice by which God punishes sinners, until he understood from Romans 1:17 that it is the righteousness God gives by faith. The Belgic Confession (1561, Article 37) calls the last judgment dreadful to the wicked but a great comfort to believers, whose innocence will be openly recognized and whose oppressors will be judged. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Question 52) teaches believers to await as judge the same person who first submitted to God's judgment for them. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 33) says the day is appointed to display God's mercy in the saved and his justice in the condemned.

In the modern period the doctrine came under pressure from two sides. Much liberal Protestant theology of the nineteenth century softened or set aside the idea of divine wrath as unworthy of a loving God. At the same time Christians recovered the Bible's link between judgment and social justice: Walter Rauschenbusch's A Theology for the Social Gospel (1917) in North America, and in Latin America the bishops' conference at Medellín (1968) and Gustavo Gutiérrez's A Theology of Liberation (1971), which read Matthew 25 as God's identification with the poor. Martin Luther King Jr. made Amos 5:24 a watchword of the American civil rights movement, in his Letter from Birmingham Jail and his speech at the March on Washington (both 1963). After the wars in the former Yugoslavia, Miroslav Volf argued in Exclusion and Embrace (1996) that belief in God's final judgment is not the enemy of peace but a condition of it, because only those who trust God to judge can lay down the sword of revenge. The site's treatment of the last things is at /theology/doctrine/last-things.

differ.view: Reformation Protestant: judged by works, justified by faith
differ.body: Lutheran and Reformed Christians hold that the believer's standing before God is settled now by faith in Christ, whose righteousness is counted to the believer and who bore God's judgment in his place (Romans 3:21-26; 8:1). The final judgment according to works (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10) does not reopen that verdict. For believers it publicly shows the genuineness of faith by its fruit, since true faith always works through love, and it assigns rewards that are themselves gifts of grace (1 Corinthians 3:14). The Heidelberg Catechism and the Westminster Confession teach this, and its defenders say it alone gives the troubled conscience a firm place to stand on the last day.

The Catholic Church teaches that justification is God's work of making a person righteous by grace, first given in baptism, and that good works done by the justified, in grace and through Christ, truly merit an increase of grace and eternal life. The Council of Trent (1547) taught this while insisting that all merit is itself God's gift, so that in crowning human merits God crowns his own gifts. On this view Romans 2:6-7 and Matthew 25 are taken at face value: God will reward the works his grace has produced. Defenders hold that this honors both grace and the real moral transformation Scripture promises, and guards against a faith that stays fruitless.

differ.view: Future justification according to the whole life
differ.body: Some Protestant scholars associated with the New Perspective on Paul, N. T. Wright most prominently, argue that Paul speaks of a present justification by faith that anticipates a future verdict given in accordance with the whole life lived, a life produced by the Spirit rather than earned. They point to Romans 2:13, where the doers of the law will be declared righteous, and to Romans 8:1-4. Defenders say this reads Paul's future judgment texts without explaining them away while keeping grace at the root. Critics within Reformed and Lutheran churches worry it unsettles assurance; Wright answers that the present verdict reliably anticipates the future one.

differ.view: One general judgment or several judgments
differ.body: Most churches, following the creeds, expect one general judgment of all people, righteous and wicked, at Christ's return (Matthew 25:31-32; John 5:28-29; Revelation 20:12), with the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10) and the great white throne as two descriptions of the same day. Dispensational interpreters distinguish several: the judgment seat of Christ for believers' rewards after the rapture, a judgment of the living nations when Christ returns (Matthew 25), and the great white throne for the unbelieving dead after the millennium (Revelation 20:11-15). They argue that the different settings and participants in these passages show different events. Both sides agree that every person gives account to Christ.

differ.view: Who are the least of these in Matthew 25
differ.body: Many readers, including much Catholic social teaching and liberation theology, take ‘the least of these brothers of Mine’ (Matthew 25:40) to mean anyone in need, so that the nations are judged by their mercy to the poor, in whom Christ is present. Others, noting that Matthew elsewhere uses ‘brothers’ and ‘little ones’ for Jesus' disciples (Matthew 10:42; 12:49-50; 28:10), read the passage as judging the nations by how they received Christ's messengers. Defenders of each reading say it keeps the passage from being cheapened: the first from shrinking mercy to a church matter, the second from turning the gospel into good deeds. Both readings agree that Christ identifies himself with the vulnerable, and that Scripture elsewhere commands mercy to all the poor.

errors:
The church has rejected the teaching that the God of judgment is a lesser or different God from the Father of Jesus, the error of Marcion. Jesus spoke of judgment more sharply than the prophets did, and the New Testament names him the judge. It has also rejected the Pelagian idea, condemned at the Council of Carthage in 418, that people can earn a favorable verdict by their own natural strength; the Bible's account of judgment is meant to silence every mouth and send sinners to grace (Romans 3:19-24). The opposite distortion, that because Christ has borne judgment the way a believer lives does not matter, runs into Paul's own warning that all will appear before Christ's judgment seat, and into James's insistence that mercy will be shown to the merciful.

Two other misuses are common. One is reading every disaster as God's specific sentence on its victims. Job's friends did this and were rebuked (Job 42:7), and Jesus refused it when told of Galileans killed by Pilate and of those crushed by a falling tower, saying they were not worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1-5; see also John 9:2-3). God does judge in history, but no one is given the right to decode which suffering is judgment on whom. The other misuse is taking God's seat: pronouncing on another person's final destiny, taking private revenge, or treating a political cause as the instrument of God's wrath. Scripture reserves final judgment and vengeance to God (Romans 12:19; 1 Corinthians 4:5), and assigns human authorities only a limited, accountable justice (Romans 13:4).
life:
Because God will judge, evil does not have the last word, and neither does the powerful person who got away with it. That is good news first for victims. The Bible gives the abused, the defrauded, and the forgotten the right to cry “How long?” and the promise of an answer, and it frees them from having to carry out justice themselves, which is often the only way a wronged person can let go of revenge without pretending the wrong did not matter. It is also sobering. Every careless word and hidden motive will come to light, and those who have been given much will be asked for much. Jesus' teaching that the judge identifies himself with the hungry, the stranger, and the prisoner turns ordinary acts of mercy into matters of eternal weight.

For the Christian, the judgment seat belongs to the one who was judged in their place. That is why the Heidelberg Catechism could speak of awaiting the judge with head lifted up. Believers can face the truth about themselves, confess sin honestly, and stop defending their record, because their hope rests on Christ's record. Yet the same judgment calls them to live now as people who will give account: fair in business, honest in speech, merciful to the weak, and slow to condemn others, since “with the same judgment you pronounce, you will be judged” (Matthew 7:2).
questions: In the Old Testament, to judge often means to rescue the oppressed as well as to condemn the oppressor. How does that change the way you hear the promise that God is coming to judge the earth?

Paul says that God will repay each person according to their deeds (Romans 2:6) and that there is no condemnation for those in Christ (Romans 8:1). How do the traditions described here hold these two statements together?

Jesus refused to say that the victims of Pilate or the falling tower were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1-5). What does that teach about how Christians should and should not speak about disasters?
